abstract: CONTEXT Precision agriculture leverages advanced technologies such as the Internet of Things (IoT) and artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance crop productivity by providing data-driven insights. In Bangladesh, optimizing crop recommendations using real-time soil and environmental data is crucial for improving agricultural decision-making. However, integrating AI models with IoT devices for instantaneous crop prediction remains a challenge due to computational constraints and the need for model interpretability. OBJECTIVE This study aims to develop an IoT-based crop prediction system that utilizes real-time data on soil nutrients, pH, and weather conditions. The system employs machine learning and deep learning techniques to recommend suitable crops based on local environmental factors. The implementation focuses on deploying the best-performing models on an edge device for real-time predictions as well as ensuring accuracy, efficiency, and accessibility for farmers and agricultural stakeholders. METHODS The system was developed in Bangladesh using proprietary data from the Soil Resource Development Institute, supported by Habiganj Agricultural University, Sylhet. The dataset consists of 3,300 samples covering 22 crops and eight soil and environmental features. Several machine learning algorithms, including Random Forest, Gradient Boosting, and Stacking ensembles, as well as deep learning models such as TabNet, were evaluated for crop prediction. The best-performing models were deployed on a Raspberry Pi 5 edge device for real-time inference. A weather API was integrated for local humidity and rainfall data, while an RS485 7-in-1 agricultural soil sensor provided real-time measurements of nitrogen (N), phosphorus (P), potassium (K), pH, temperature, and soil moisture. The predictions were displayed on the ThingsBoard IoT platform. Model interpretability was enhanced using the explainable AI technique LIME. A user survey involving farmers, agricultural researchers, and students assessed the usability, accuracy, and reliability of the system. RESULTS AND CONCLUSIONS The highest accuracy among machine learning models was achieved using Random Forest (95.8%) and Gradient Boosting (95.5%). The Stacking ensemble technique, with Support Vector Classifier (SVC) as the meta-classifier, achieved the highest overall accuracy of 95.9%. Among deep learning models, TabNet performed best with an accuracy of 92%. The Random Forest model was selected for deployment on the Raspberry Pi due to its lowest inference time and compatibility with Python and TensorFlow Lite. User feedback from the survey provided insights into the system's practical effectiveness and potential areas for improvement. The results demonstrate that integrating AI-driven crop recommendation models with IoT devices can support real-time agricultural decision-making, improving precision farming outcomes. SIGNIFICANCE This study contributes to precision agriculture by demonstrating an IoT-based crop prediction system that integrates AI-driven recommendations with real-time environmental monitoring. The deployment of the best-performing model on an edge device ensures accessibility and efficiency for users in agricultural settings. By leveraging explainable AI techniques, the study enhances model interpretability, fostering trust and usability among farmers and agricultural researchers. The findings highlight the potential of AI and IoT in improving crop selection, optimizing resource usage, and supporting sustainable agricultural practices in Bangladesh and beyond. The implementation code and private dataset are available at: https://github.com/SAIFULLAH-SHARAFAT/An-IoT-Enabled-AI-System-for-Real-Time-Crop-Prediction-Using-Soil-and-Weather-Data.

abstract: Water scarcity is a growing global challenge, particularly in arid and semi-arid regions, where climate change is increasing both the frequency and intensity of droughts. Irrigated agriculture accounts for about 70 % of global freshwater withdrawals, but its expansion remains crucial for enhancing local socio-economic stability and development, and for increasing food production to meet the needs of an ever-increasing global population. Consequently, improving irrigation efficiency is an increasingly important goal to promote sustainable development and environmental sustainability while simultaneously minimizing or avoiding any negative impact on crop yields. In Spain, most irrigated areas have adopted pressurized irrigation systems to increase irrigation efficiency. In this context, precision irrigation, which aims to supply plants with exactly the water they need at the right time and place, or at times that minimize the negative impact on crop production, is becoming increasingly essential. However, the intricate interactions among plants, soil, and the atmosphere make accurately determining crop water needs, both in real-time and for future scenarios, a persistent challenge and an active area of research. This complexity makes it more difficult for farmers to decide when and how much water to apply, thereby hindering the optimization of irrigation practices. To address this, advanced tools are essential to enable farmers to easily and accurately estimate crop water requirements across past, present, and future scenarios, while also facilitating effective irrigation scheduling adapted to diverse irrigation strategies. This thesis is organized into six chapters, focused on the development of technological tools to enhance irrigation efficiency through precision irrigation strategies. Chapter 1 provides the context and rationale for the thesis, leading to the objectives outlined in Chapter 2. Chapter 3 outlines the development of an Internet of Things (IoT) platform for smart irrigation systems. The platform has been built using FIWARE, a widely adopted European standard that facilitates seamless integration with various other platforms. A custom-designed datalogger, equipped with soil moisture sensors, was incorporated to monitor soil moisture and simulate the water needs of an olive farm located in Cordoba, Spain. This simulation of olive grove water needs was based on a soil water balance model, using the dual crop coefficient to calculate crop evapotranspiration. To demonstrate the platform’s practical application, a deficit irrigation strategy was employed, highlighting its effectiveness when water resources are scarce. In Chapter 4, a new IoT system is developed to further enhance the existing IoT platform. This system integrates edge-computing technology with RGB cameras and the AquaCrop model, a model developed by FAO that simulates the yield response of herbaceous crops to water, being particularly suitable for conditions where water is a limiting factor. One of AquaCrop’s key strengths is its ability to estimate crop yield based on applied irrigation schedules, making it particularly valuable for designing deficit irrigation strategies. Since AquaCrop relies on the development of canopy cover to simulate crop growth, the integration of RGB cameras allows for real-time calculation of canopy cover through image-based segmentation techniques based on vegetation indices. This enables the system to dynamically adjust the AquaCrop outputs based on actual crop conditions, leading to more accurate and efficient irrigation scheduling. The system was successfully tested on a wheat crop at a commercial farm in Cordoba, Spain, demonstrating its benefits to apply in real-time irrigation scheduling. When using RGB-based vegetation indices, canopy cover calculations must be performed at solar noon, to minimize errors caused by shadows and ensure consistent lighting conditions. To overcome this limitation and allow the system to capture images at any time, Chapter 5 presents the development of a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) capable of autonomously calculating canopy cover under varying conditions. The CNN was optimized using a genetic algorithm NSGA-II and trained on thousands of images of wheat, pepper, and alfalfa crops, in Andalusia, Spain, and California, USA. The optimization process focused on two primary objectives: minimizing the prediction error and reducing the network’s complexity. A lightweight model was essential to ensure compatibility with the previously developed edge-computing system. Results showed that the low-density CNN could predict canopy cover with an R2 of 0.98 and a Mean Absolute Error of 0.038. Finally, Chapter 6 summarizes key conclusions drawn from the development of this thesis and explores potential directions for future research. By integrating real-time sensor data, weather forecasting APIs, irrigation scheduling models, and artificial intelligence, this thesis highlights the importance of smart irrigation strategies and develops several tools to improve, automate, and facilitate real-time and future simulation of irrigation scheduling based on plant water needs and expected yields.

abstract: This thesis investigates porous silicon (pSi) as a CMOS-compatible nanoporous ion-exchange membrane for nanofluidic reverse electrodialysis (nRED), with the long-term objective of enabling miniaturized salinity-gradient energy harvesters for autonomous microsystems and low-power IoT platforms. While conventional reverse electrodialysis relies on dense polymer ion-exchange membranes optimized for large-scale stacks, nanofluidic approaches exploit surface-charge-governed ion transport in nanoscale pores and offer a possible route toward microfabricated energy conversion devices. However, despite promising results at the single-pore level, the translation of such concepts into integrable membrane technologies remains limited, and porous silicon had not previously been investigated as an active membrane material for nRED. To address this gap, the thesis combines theoretical analysis, numerical modeling, membrane fabrication, and experimental benchmarking. A physics-based model of ionic transport in charged nanopores under salinity gradients was first developed to determine how pore radius, porosity, and surface charge density affect permselectivity, ionic resistance, and output power. The simulations revealed a fundamental trade-off between selectivity and conductance and identified a fabrication window in which pores below about 20 nm are expected to be favorable at the membrane scale. Based on these insights, porous silicon membranes were fabricated and tested in a custom reverse electrodialysis platform. Two fabrication routes were explored. A self-supported approach proved unsuitable because the final DRIE step altered pore opening and induced unstable, rectifying electrical behavior. A second route based on electropolishing lift-off enabled the fabrication of free-standing membranes with preserved porous structure and stable I–V characteristics suitable for RED characterization. Their experimental response followed the qualitative trends predicted by the numerical model, confirming that ionic transport is governed by surface-charge-dominated nanofluidic effects. Most importantly, this work demonstrates for the first time that porous silicon can function as an ion-selective membrane for nanofluidic reverse electrodialysis. Under the tested conditions, the best free-standing membrane achieved a maximum power density of about 1.33 mW/m2. To further improve performance, hybrid membranes combining a thin selective active layer with a thicker support layer werefabricated, and an adaptive surface-charge regulation model was introduced to better capture the coupling between surface chemistry and ion transport. Although these developments improved physical understanding and highlighted viable optimization routes, they also showed that substantial limitations remain, especially regarding surface-charge modeling, membrane resistance, and practical upscaling. Overall, the thesis establishes porous silicon as a new platform for selective ion transport in nRED and provides the first integrated framework linking pore design, fabrication, electrochemical benchmarking, and numerical interpretation. Beyond salinity-gradient energy harvesting, the results open perspectives for porous silicon in iontronic, sensing, and lab-on-chip applications where CMOS compatibility and nanoscale control are decisive advantages.

abstract: This Undergraduate Thesis Portfolio brings together both a technical capstone project and a Science, Technology, and Society (STS) research paper, each addressing different dimensions of sustainability and accessibility within the built environment. The capstone project focuses on disability concerns related to impaired mobility and independence, aiming to make an individual’s environment more inclusive and responsive to their needs through technological innovation. In parallel, the STS research paper examines sustainability in the construction industry, questioning whether current policies and practices adequately address environmental, economic, and social outcomes across a building’s lifecycle. While one project is rooted in hands-on design and the other in systems-based analysis, both are connected through a shared emphasis on improving how people interact with and benefit from built spaces. Together, these works highlight that sustainability extends beyond environmental performance to include social and functional accessibility, ensuring that spaces are not only efficient but also equitable and inclusive. The capstone project, G.L.A.S.S. (Glasses for Linked Automation of Smart Systems), is a smart glasses control system designed to improve accessibility and independence for individuals interacting with smart devices. Modern smart homes are filled with connected technologies, yet for individuals with mobility impairments, tasks such as adjusting lights or operating entertainment systems can remain challenging. This system provides a hands-free method for controlling devices using intuitive hand gestures. The core of the system is a microcontroller-based processing unit that interprets hand gestures from a front-facing camera mounted on the glasses. Users can look toward a device within their field of vision to connect, and gestures are translated into commands through Wi-Fi or Bluetooth communication. The system is designed for flexibility, allowing users to add new devices, map gestures to specific functions, and receive interactive feedback through an overlaid display. By increasing compatibility across devices and enabling control of technologies such as smart lights, televisions, and computers, the project aims to enhance user experience and serve as a scalable, hands-free interface for IoT technologies. The STS research paper examines the effectiveness of sustainable construction policies and practices in the United States compared to those in other countries, with a focus on identifying barriers to improved environmental, economic, and social outcomes. While buildings account for a significant portion of national energy consumption and tools such as LEED and life-cycle assessment methods have been developed to guide sustainable design, the United States continues to face challenges in achieving consistent results. This research argues that these challenges are not due to a lack of capability but rather stem from gaps in knowledge and inconsistent understanding across stakeholders. Public awareness of sustainability issues remains low, and even within the construction industry, designers and constructors may lack the knowledge necessary to implement the most effective solutions. Additionally, misconceptions about the cost of green buildings discourage owners from adopting sustainable practices, despite evidence that such designs can improve efficiency, productivity, and overall building performance. By emphasizing these knowledge and perception gaps, the paper highlights the need for more integrated approaches that align education, practice, and policy to achieve more effective sustainability outcomes. Working on both the capstone and STS projects simultaneously reinforced that sustainability challenges are not caused by a lack of available technologies, but by disconnects in knowledge, priorities, and implementation across systems. The capstone project demonstrated how technical innovation, such as G.L.A.S.S., can directly improve social sustainability by increasing accessibility and independence, while the STS research showed that gaps in education, stakeholder understanding, and policy enforcement limit the effectiveness of sustainable practices in the construction industry. Through the capstone, I developed technical and collaborative skills, particularly in integrating complex systems, resolving software incompatibilities, and making design decisions under time and resource constraints, while the STS work expanded my understanding of how similar coordination challenges exist at a societal level among designers, constructors, and policymakers. Together, these experiences highlighted that meaningful sustainability requires both well-designed technologies and the broader systems that support their adoption, emphasizing that innovation and implementation must work together to achieve outcomes that are not only efficient but also equitable and impactful.

abstract: The architecture, engineering and construction (AEC) industry is undergoing a significant digital change. Artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, digital twins, extended reality (XR), cyber-physical systems (CPS) and data-driven modelling are all trying to make the built environments more sustainable and efficient (Adu-Amankwa et al., 2023; Pour Rahimian et al., 2020).The construction industry continues to operate under many different pressures. Projects must be cost-effective, energy-efficient, operationally resilient and safe for workers and occupants. Traditional methods of managing projects, monitoring safety, estimating costs and maintaining infrastructure are inadequate for today’s complex needs (Najafi et al., 2024). Persistent issues, such as budget overruns, workplace injuries, high energy consumption, a lack of data transparency and ageing assets, highlight the need for better solutions (Azis et al., 2012; Najafi et al., 2024; Rodriguez Trejo et al., 2024).While digital technologies and tools are progressing rapidly, their adoption in the construction industry remains uneven. The industry still struggles with fragmented data systems, poor interoperability, organisational inertia, limited integration strategies and uncertainty around returns on investment (Chen et al., 2023; Kumar Singh et al., 2023). These barriers continue to slow progress toward a fully digital and connected construction ecosystem.This issue of Smart and Sustainable Built Environment looks at these critical challenges. It shows how digital innovation can enhance the built environment at every stage of its lifecycle. This collection features cutting-edge research that demonstrates its practical applications in various fields, including smart cities, construction safety, cost estimation, energy efficiency, facilities management (FM) and infrastructure monitoring. The papers together demonstrate how new ideas are being applied; AI-driven pose analysis helps prevent musculoskeletal injuries on construction sites. Deep learning models predict bridge deterioration. Blockchain enables transparent project monitoring. Optimised window design reduces hospital cooling loads. Smart city technologies enhance disaster management and response to public health crises. Collectively, these papers showcase the transformative potential of digital technologies in practice. Next, we take a closer look at each contribution.Purushothaman and Gedara (2025) present a smart vision-based method (SVBM), an AI-driven approach that uses computer vision through recorded and live videos from mobile and embedded cameras to analyse human poses during manual lifting in construction. The study applies a pragmatic research approach supported by a literature review and lab validation. SVBM can detect and analyse postures without using wearable sensors, comparing body movements to standard axes to identify abnormal positions. It calculates joint and body part angles using novel software and a mobile application, operating in both real-time and offline modes. The system helps predict and prevent posture-related risks before injuries occur, improving safety and health in the construction sector. Although limitations exist, such as restricted database access and unaddressed privacy concerns, SVBM offers substantial practical benefits. It enables realistic analysis of human movement, advancing research on musculoskeletal disorder prevention and promoting a healthier, more safety-conscious workforce.In another study, Atapattu et al. (2025) explore statistical modelling techniques to improve cost estimation and reduce cost overruns in infrastructure projects. Using a bibliographic literature review, the study analysed publications through keyword co-occurrence and trend mapping with VOS-Viewer. Seven main cost-modelling techniques were identified: regression analysis (RA), artificial neural networks (ANNs), case-based reasoning (CBR), fuzzy logic, Monte Carlo simulation, support vector machines and reference class forecasting. Among these, RA, ANN and CBR were the most widely studied. The results show that combining two or more methods can enhance model performance. The study offers practical insights for industry professionals seeking to improve traditional estimation methods.Almhafdy and Alsehail (2025) examine how optimising window design factors (WDFs) can reduce cooling loads in hospital buildings. They have focused on government hospitals in the arid climate of Saudi Arabia’s Qassim region. Almhafdy and Alsehail (2025) investigate key WDFs such as window-to-wall ratio (WWR), window orientation, room size and glazing U-value to identify design conditions that minimise energy consumption and comply with the Saudi Building Code (SBC). Data were collected using a smart weather station, and simulations were conducted through Integrated Environmental Solution Virtual Environment software. Results show that larger patient rooms are approximately 40% more energy-efficient than smaller ones, with those facing north consuming less energy. The analysis also revealed that some WWR and U-value combinations fail to meet SBC energy standards, which emphasises the need for proper compliance. The study highlights the importance of optimising glazing properties and window ratios according to building orientation and climate to ensure energy efficiency, reduce costs and support sustainable hospital design.In their study, Teo et al. (2025) focus on improving WiFi signal strength estimation for smart home applications by accounting for building morphology. Traditional log-based path loss models often fail to predict signal strength accurately across different house types because they overlook structural variations. To address this, the study proposes a new decision tree-based path loss model developed from measurements of WiFi signals passing through multiple housing units. Three regression models were tested and compared. Results show that while the traditional log-based model works well for small houses, the new nonlinear model performs better in larger homes with areas over 125 m2 and an area-to-perimeter ratio above 2.5. The study confirms and quantifies the influence of building design on signal propagation. By incorporating these factors, the proposed model significantly improves indoor network coverage prediction, supporting more reliable smart home applications.In another interesting study, Gutierrez-Bucheli et al. (2025) explore how XR technologies can be effectively integrated into vocational education and training for the construction sector. The authors argue that although the use of XR in education is growing, there is limited understanding of how to align these technologies with tailored teaching approaches. In this study, Gutierrez-Bucheli et al. (2025) combine an in-depth literature review with the Delphi technique, including expert group discussions and follow-up questionnaires, to identify key decision-making factors. The results show that institutional factors are the most critical for successful XR adoption, followed by training and technology considerations. This research highlights the need for future studies to evaluate XR performance after implementation to understand its cost, value and long-term impact.In their study, Renukappa et al. (2025) explore how India’s Smart Cities Mission contributed to managing the COVID-19 outbreak across more than 2000 cities. Despite the global and national impact of the pandemic, little research has explored the role of smart city strategies in health crisis management within developing countries. Conducting a literature review and semi-structured interviews, this study investigates how selected smart cities in India responded to the pandemic. Findings highlight six key strategies used to manage the crisis: integrated command and control centres, AI and app-based solutions, smart waste management, smart healthcare management, smart data management and smart surveillance. Each city faced unique challenges but adapted these technologies to local needs. The study offers valuable insights for policymakers, introducing the “six Cs” framework – crisis management leadership, credible communication, collaboration, creative governance, capturing knowledge and capacity building – to guide future preparedness and improve smart city resilience in developing contexts.In another research, Lafhaj et al. (2025) present the COPULA framework, a blockchain-based solution designed to improve construction project monitoring by enhancing efficiency, transparency and trust. The framework leverages the decentralised and secure nature of blockchain to address key challenges in project management, such as data centralisation, privacy and security issues. This study develops the COPULA model using the blockchain and evaluates its performance through detailed testing of execution cost, time, data integrity, immutability and security. A case study reveals its practical application and benefits in real-world construction scenarios. The results show that COPULA enables seamless and tamper-proof data exchange among stakeholders, ensuring real-time transparency and stronger collaboration. While future research is needed to explore its integration with existing project management systems and scalability across different project types, this study provides a complete, validated digital framework. COPULA represents a major step forward in applying blockchain for construction management and offers a practical and innovative tool for digital transformation in the sector.Habib et al. (2025) introduce a blockchain-based framework for improving earthquake disaster management in smart cities. The authors argue that traditional seismic risk management systems often suffer from centralisation, limited transparency and slow response times. To address these issues, Habib et al. (2025) propose an innovative seismic monitoring and automated decision-support system built on blockchain technology. This framework integrates real-time seismic data within a decentralised blockchain network, ensuring accuracy, reliability and security. Smart contracts are used to automate decision-making and trigger rapid responses during emergencies. The findings show that this system enhances reliability, efficiency and collaboration among stakeholders, enabling faster and more coordinated disaster responses. By leveraging blockchain’s strengths – decentralised control, data integrity and automation – this study demonstrates how digital innovation can transform conventional disaster management practices. The proposed framework provides a foundation for applying blockchain in other disaster response contexts, which paves the way for more transparent and resilient smart city systems.Mohandes et al. (2025) explore the barriers to implementing digital twin technology in construction projects, with a focus on enhancing operational performance and sustainability. Although DTs are widely recognised for supporting sustainable construction, their adoption remains limited in many countries. In their study, Mohandes et al. (2025) first identify common barriers through a literature review and then validate them through a questionnaire survey of professionals in Hong Kong’s construction industry. Results reveal key barriers, including the lack of methodologies and tools, challenges in maintaining real-time communication performance, difficulties in measuring all relevant data, the need to share DTs across multiple systems and stakeholders and uncertainties in data quality and reliability. The statistical analysis confirmed that data-sharing challenges among stakeholders are particularly significant. Practically, the findings provide clear guidance for overcoming these barriers to improve cost efficiency, sustainability and competitiveness in construction.In another study, Stas and Abrishami (2025) explore how emerging technologies and modern management approaches can transform collaboration and efficiency in the AEC industry. As the sector undergoes rapid digital change, the study investigates the integration of building information modelling (BIM), blockchain and the Internet of Things with management techniques such as work breakdown structure (WBS) and agile thinking. Using a literature review to develop a conceptual framework and an exploratory questionnaire for validation, the research demonstrates that combining blockchain with WBS and BIM can create more transparent, secure and efficient workflows. This integrated approach enhances collaboration and overcomes many limitations of traditional building practices. The findings highlight how such technological and managerial synergies can improve productivity, quality and cost-effectiveness while supporting sustainable and trustworthy project delivery.Ikuabe et al. (2025) investigate the key factors driving the adoption of CPS in FM, aiming to enhance efficiency and digital transformation in post-occupancy operations. Adopting a deductive, post-positivist approach, the study used a quantitative research design supported by a structured questionnaire. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, the Kruskal–Wallis H-test, exploratory factor analysis and confirmatory factor analysis. Results show strong model validity and reveal that key drivers for CPS adoption include adequate resource allocation for system procurement, top management commitment, system stability and compatibility with existing systems. These factors are essential for encouraging organisations to integrate CPS into their FM practices. The study provides practical guidance for industry leaders seeking to improve operational performance through digital technologies. It is also the first empirical investigation to identify and evaluate the main enablers of CPS adoption for FM using second-order multivariate analysis, contributing valuable insights to both research and practice in digital construction management.In this study, Oke et al. (2025) present a capability assessment model and self-appraisal tool to help heavy construction firms evaluate their readiness for digital transformation. Recognising the importance of digital adoption for industrial growth and competitiveness, the study applies the technology–organisation–environment (TOE) and natural resource dependence theory frameworks to identify 22 markers for evaluating digital capabilities. A questionnaire was distributed to construction professionals, and descriptive analysis alongside fuzzy synthetic evaluation (FSE) was used to develop the assessment model. Key findings highlight five critical markers: leadership commitment to digital transformation, workforce readiness, potential ROI through efficiency gains, technology maturity and the complexity of integrating new technologies with existing workflows. FSE analysis further emphasised technology, organisational and resource optimisation as the most influential factors. The study offers a practical, validated self-appraisal tool that enables heavy construction firms to monitor and enhance their digital transformation efforts, bridging theory and practice in digital readiness assessment.Finally, Abu Dabous et al. (2025) develop deep-learning models to predict the deterioration of concrete bridge decks, addressing the critical need for regular inspection and maintenance to ensure public safety and sustainable transport services. Three models – vanilla LSTM (vLSTM), stacked LSTM and CNN-LSTM – were trained using the National Bridge Inventory (NBI) datasets from 2001 to 2019 to forecast deck condition ratings for 2021. All models achieved over 90% accuracy, with mean squared errors between 0.081 and 0.103, while CNN-LSTM performed best, reaching 93% accuracy, a correlation coefficient of 0.91 and an R2 of 0.83. This study includes a thorough data cleansing process to address limitations in the NBI database and provides a framework for implementing AI-based models for maintenance planning. This research offers a practical guideline for leveraging bridge inventory datasets to improve deterioration prediction, with potential for extension to other databases and construction industry applications.

title: Desarrollo de Firmware y despliegue en entornos reales de dispositivos IoT para riego inteligente en el contexto de ciudades inteligentes

abstract: El Trabajo de Fin de Máster aquí presentado expone el desarrollo de firmware, integración y despliegue en entornos reales de dispositivos IoT enfocados al riego inteligente en el contexto de las ciudades inteligentes. Este trabajo se efectúa dentro de una iniciativa más amplia de digitalización urbana relacionada con Madrid Digital, el Ayuntamiento de Madrid y el laboratorio IoTMadLab del CeDInt, de la Universidad Politécnica de Madrid. Principalmente, se busca contribuir a la creación de una infraestructura urbana capaz de monitorizar recursos distribuidos, transmitir información en tiempo real y actuar sobre ellos de forma eficiente. Se aborda tanto el diseño como la implementación, validación y despliegue de dos dispositivos principales: el Earthmeter y el Watercontroller. Por un lado, el Earthmeter es un dispositivo de sensorización que tiene como objetivo la medición de ciertas variables del terreno regable como la temperatura, la humedad del suelo y, en algunos casos, el pH. Por otra parte, el Watercontroller combina capacidad de actuación, pudiendo gestionar electroválvulas para controlar el riego, y sensorización, pudiendo medir el volumen de agua que se utiliza en cada ciclo de riego, mediante el uso de caudalímetros. Estos dispositivos permiten construir una solución integrada de monitorización y actuación, en la que el estado del terreno y el consumo de agua pueden ser observados y gestionados de forma remota. Una de las piezas clave de este trabajo es el uso de ciertos protocolos concretos especialmente convenientes para una arquitectura IoT urbana. Estos destacan por enfocarse en conseguir un bajo consumo y garantizar la interoperabilidad. Los protocolos y formatos que se utilizan son IEEE 802.15.4, 6LoWPAN, RPL, IPv6, UDP, CoAP, LwM2M, objetos OMA, CBOR y SenML, componiendo la pila de red utilizada. Esto permite que los dispositivos se puedan comunicar en una red inalámbrica específicamente diseñada para entornos urbanos, en la que cada uno de ellos tiene la capacidad de direccionamiento individual y de tener un bajo consumo energético, además una representación estandarizada de los datos. La estandarización es un factor crucial en este contexto, ya que facilita que dispositivos desarrollados por cualquier organización tengan la posibilidad de integrarse dentro de una infraestructura común en una ciudad inteligente. Para el desarrollo de firmware, que toma un papel principal en este trabajo, se programan microcontroladores en placas hechas a medida para su propósito, teniendo que desarrollar funcionalidad tanto para comunicación inalámbrica como cableada. En el caso del Earthmeter, se implementa la comunicación con sensores, pudiendo usar múltiples, mediante Modbus sobre RS-485, permitiendo las lecturas del terreno ya mencionadas. En el caso del Watercontroller, se ha desarrollado la lógica necesaria para gestionar electroválvulas, caudalímetros y la comunicación entre microcontroladores mediante UART. Otra parte importante en el desarrollo de código ha sido la definición de estructuras de datos, objetos OMA y mecanismos de envío de información hacia el CMS. Todo esto se hace resolviendo problemas asociados a la compatibilidad y representación de datos, presentando también las limitaciones que implican el uso de herramientas propietarias. Todos los datos que estos dispositivos envían tienen como destino el CMS, de la empresa Paradox, donde se centralizan. El CMS se utiliza para todo tipo de actividades en la monitorización y gestión de la red, y es una herramienta fundamental en este proyecto. Se utiliza para consultar el estado de los equipos, analizar datos recibidos y ejecutar acciones remotas, todo esto gracias a la comunicación basada en objetos OMA. Se usa también Home Assistant como interfaz complementaria para mejorar la visualización y facilitar el control de los dispositivos en proyectos piloto concretos, ya que permite un grado más alto de personalización, pudiendo generar paneles a medida. Esta centralización permite que los datos de riego formen parte de una visión del conjunto de la ciudad, reforzando la trazabilidad, la supervisión y la soberanía sobre la información que provee la infraestructura desplegada. Una faceta que guía parte del trabajo es la idea del bajo consumo energético. Se estudian versiones convencionales y versiones optimizadas de los dispositivos, las cuales incorporan distintas estrategias como el uso de modos de bajo consumo, activación periódica mediante RTC, protecciones para mantener despierto el sistema durante tareas críticas y la posibilidad de alimentación mediante batería y panel solar. Este enfoque resulta de gran utilidad para facilitar despliegues prolongados en ubicaciones donde no existe alimentación eléctrica continua, reduciendo las necesidades de mantenimiento y favoreciendo soluciones más sostenibles, lo cual puede ser adecuado dentro del contexto estudiado. La validación del sistema se ha realizado tanto en laboratorio como en entornos reales, destacando el despliegue en el CIEC, Centro de Innovación en Economía Circular. Durante estas pruebas se han analizado aspectos como la conectividad, la comunicación con sensores, el envío de múltiples instancias de datos y la recepción de órdenes remotas de actuación, verificando que los componentes tuvieran conexiones fiables. También se estudia si otros aspectos operan satisfactoriamente como, por ejemplo, la actuación sobre electroválvulas, la medición del consumo de agua, la representación en plataformas de visualización y el comportamiento de las versiones de bajo consumo. El despliegue real ha permitido explorar cuáles son los problemas propios de escenarios urbanos, como limitaciones de conectividad, integración con sistemas cerrados y dificultades derivadas de la instalación física de los dispositivos. Como resultado, el proyecto demuestra la viabilidad de una solución IoT aplicada al riego inteligente en el contexto de una infraestructura urbana real. Se consigue cumplir con la funcionalidad deseada, exponiendo el desempeño de los dispositivos. De este modo, el trabajo contribuye a una gestión más eficiente de los recursos hídricos y energéticos, y sienta las bases para futuros despliegues a mayor escala en Madrid. Finalmente, se plantean líneas de trabajo futuro relacionadas con la implementación propia del transceptor, la mejora de la autonomía energética, la ampliación de instalaciones de riego y el despliegue progresivo de dispositivos en una red urbana de mayor escala. En conjunto, este Trabajo de Fin de Máster constituye una aportación práctica al desarrollo de ciudades inteligentes, combinando firmware embebido, redes IoT de bajo consumo, estandarización de datos, actuación remota y validación en entornos reales. title: Standards-Compliant Zero Trust Framework-Based Software-Defined Perimeter (SDP) for Securing Residential IoT Networks

abstract: The proliferation of consumer Internet of Things (IoT) devices has significantly expanded the attack surface of residential networks, exposing them to misconfigurations, excessive permissions, and lateral movement threats. This paper presents a novel Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA) that integrates Manufacturer Usage Description (MUD) policies with a Software-Defined Perimeter (SDP) enforcement framework to secure consumer-grade IoT environments. Our approach enables automated, context-aware access control through device-specific policy generation, WireGuard-based encrypted tunnels, and dynamic micro-segmentation enforced at the IoT gateway. We implement and evaluate the system on a Raspberry Pi-based testbed, demonstrating a 78% reduction in manual configuration time and effective real-time enforcement of least-privilege policies. Security evaluations confirm full prevention of unauthorized lateral traffic and rapid reaction to policy violations. The architecture adheres to secure-by-default principles and aligns with emerging standards such as RFC 8520 and the EU Cyber Resilience Act, offering a scalable and standards-compliant path to Zero Trust in residential IoT deployments.

abstract: As smart home technologies evolve, achieving energy-efficient indoor climate management while maintaining comfort and air quality is a growing priority. This paper introduces a novel optimization framework for smart buildings that minimizes energy costs and dynamically manages indoor environmental conditions, specifically temperature, CO2concentration, and illuminance. Unlike conventional systems, our model incorporates dynamic constraints that respond to day-night comfort requirements and leverage real-time variations in electricity prices and environmental conditions. By optimally controlling the power levels of air conditioning, air purification, and lighting systems, the framework ensures indoor comfort while significantly reducing operational costs.A nonlinear optimization approach with dynamic constraints is applied across a 24-hour horizon with 15-minute intervals, supported by an integrated battery storage system to balance peak demands. The model also maximizes the use of harvested energy to further enhance efficiency. Experimental results show that the proposed dynamic framework outperforms standard control methods by achieving substantial energy savings, maintaining stable indoor conditions, and effectively using renewable energy storage. Compared and validated with baseline energy consumption scenarios, this model represents a significant advancement for smart home energy management, offering a scalable and sustainable solution that adapts seamlessly to various operational and environmental conditions.

title: Improving Network Reliability in IoT- Based Home Automation Using Active Redundancy Technique

abstract: The rapid expansion of Internet of Things (IoT)-based home automation has increased the demand for network reliability, scalability, and fault tolerance in residential environments. Conventional rule-based or single-broker communication systems tend to have single points of failure, lack flexibility, and poor energy efficiency. To overcome these shortcomings, the current paper presents an active redundancy scheme (ChatRedIoT), embedded in a layered IoT framework of smart home automation. The architecture uses the multi-agent chatbot orchestration, dual-broker clustering, and predictive AI algorithms in order to provide resilient functioning, proactive fault anticipation, and smooth failover. Sensor and actuator data streams are processed on-site to generate low-latency responses and analyzed in the cloud to offer predictive analytics and optimization. The methodology uses mathematical modeling of reliability measures, such as failure rate, packet loss ratio, and Bayesian failure prediction, together with energy optimization goals. Experimental confirmation under Raspberry Pi nodes and extensive NS-3 simulation shows considerable improvements, sub-25 ms latency, fewer than 1 % packet loss, over 99.9 % of availability, and a reduction of up to 15% of the energy with indoor comfort. The findings validate the claim that active redundancy-based on predictive intelligence provides a strong and scalable base to future IoT-based smart home automation systems.

title: A systematic survey of post-matter smart-home mesh security: Commissioning, routing, and control-plane trust

abstract: The post-Matter smart home is an ad-hoc mesh network built on IEEE 802.15.4, Thread, Zigbee, Bluetooth Low Energy mesh, and Wi-Fi EasyMesh, unified at the application layer by Matter fabrics and border routers. Security in this environment is a multi-hop, multi-protocol problem, yet existing surveys either predate Matter or treat the household as a protocol-agnostic attack catalogue, leaving commissioning trust, mesh routing vulnerabilities, MAC/PHY threats, and border-router trust concentration without unified treatment. We present a systematic survey of smart-home mesh security (January 2019 to March 2026) following the PRISMA 2020 reporting framework, drawing on 241 records from IEEE Xplore, ACM DL, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, DBLP, and standards portals, each coded along fifteen dimensions covering protocol layer, attack class, defence class, and evaluation method. Six recurring findings emerge from the synthesis: (i) post-Matter commissioning reshapes rather than removes onboarding trust, concentrating the attack surface at the controller; (ii) mesh routing attacks from MANET/WSN literature remain applicable but require border-router-aware revision for post-Matter fabric interactions; (iii) 802.15.4 MAC/PHY threats transfer directly to constrained Thread and Zigbee nodes; (iv) Thread and Matter border routers concentrate cross-fabric trust in ways prior hub-centric surveys did not capture; (v) encrypted traffic analysis and RF side-channels sustain privacy leakage despite link-layer confidentiality; and (vi) learning-based intrusion detection for constrained nodes remains fragmented across incompatible datasets and threat models. Contributions include a cross-layer attack and defence taxonomy, a key-management comparison across Thread, Zigbee, BLE mesh, and Matter, an IDS dataset inventory, and a prioritised research agenda on multi-hop trust propagation, border-router hardening, and federated intrusion detection for constrained mesh nodes.

title: Sharing Can be Threatening: Uncovering Security Flaws of RBAC Model on Smart Home Platforms
venue: IEEE Transactions on Dependable and Secure Computing

abstract: The “sharing” feature provided by smart home platforms enables multiple users to access the device simultaneously with different roles and permissions, but it also presents new security challenges for the design and implementation of the permission management. The key issue is that the platform adopts two different permission assignments on the app side and the cloud side, and these two assignments must maintain consistency in authorizing. Unfortunately, real-world smart home platforms may not be able to ensure this when implementing RBAC (Role-Based Access Control) model. The inconsistency between these assignments may lead to security vulnerabilities, which can be easily exploited by malicious users. Although many existing studies have revealed security issues with smart home platforms, less attention has been paid to the sharing feature and permission assignments, as well as security issues that arise from this. In this work, we conducted a systematic study on the RBAC model and permission management of smart home platforms. To overcome technical challenges imposed by the “black-box” platform, we also proposed a novel testing framework. By testing 10 smart home platforms that all belong to the “device-connected, black-box, and multi-user supported” category, we collected each platform's “configurable permission assignment” and inferred “enforced permission assignment”. At last, we identified 44 inconsistencies that could lead to security vulnerabilities. Malicious users could exploit these vulnerabilities to initiate attacks such as device hijacking, unauthorized access, illegal control, and eavesdropping. We promptly reported these vulnerabilities to vendors and CNVD, and proposed mitigation measures.

abstract: The reactive nature of home maintenance services provision in emerging countries results in the repair of domestic appliances only after expensive breakages happen. In this study, we introduce SmartFix-AI - an intelligent maintenance extension to a bi-platform home service marketplace with the help of machine learning, aimed at facilitating predictive fault detection for diverse hardware platforms in the household sector. We propose a generalized anomaly detection pipeline which uses multisource Internet-of-Things sensor data covering seven different maintenance areas: appliance power monitoring, HVAC, leak detection, smart home activity tracking, equipment degradation, fire/smoke safety, and electrical fault detection. In order to find out the comparative performance of three anomaly detection algorithms, we conducted systematic experiments by applying them to seven open benchmark datasets, among which was the state-of-the-art C-MAPSS benchmark from NASA, using 10-fold stratified cross-validation with statistical significance verification. Our experimental results reveal the domain-specificity of the algorithms: the Transformer achieves almost perfect fault detection accuracy in the area of electrical faults $(\mathbf{F 1}=\mathbf{0. 9 6 7}$ plus or minus 0.005, AUC=0.998), whereas the LSTM Autoencoder shows the best results in equipment degradation prediction $(\mathbf{F} \mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0. 7 9 8}$ plus or minus 0.013, AUC=0.977). The Isolation Forest demonstrates the best performance in appliance monitoring $(\mathbf{F} \mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0. 5 3 8}$ plus or minus 0.026) and strong performance in electrical fault detection $(\mathbf{F} \mathbf{1}=\mathbf{0. 9 3 4}$ plus or minus $\mathbf{0. 0 1 7})$. Statistical significance is established in all 21 pairs of algorithm comparison (p less than 0.005, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). The proposed SmartFix-AI framework sends pro-active maintenance alarms in the framework of our Flutter mobile application and Next.js dashboard.

abstract: This paper presents a computationally efficient, localized Digital Twin (DT) framework engineered for real-time state tracking and thermal protection of low-voltage DC motors operating under dynamic load conditions. Traditional edge-monitoring systems rely heavily on static threshold alerts, which fail to capture non-linear degradation characteristics. To address this limitation, the proposed architecture deploys an embedded cyber-physical framework using an ESP32 edge-node integrated with an algorithmic Virtual Twin layer running via Node-RED. The Virtual Twin evaluates a dynamic state observer model alongside an enhanced thermal Arrhenius relationship to continuously track the battery State of Charge (SoC) and winding temperature concurrently. Real-time telemetry is transmitted over a lightweight, local messaging topology to ensure seamless bidirectional actuation. Experimental evaluations demonstrate a total fault isolation latency of 34 ms during critical thermal anomalies, proving that the system successfully mitigates cascading power cell destruction within resource-constrained Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) applications.

title: Zero-Day Attack Detection in IoT Networks Using Graph Neural Networks and Online Learning

abstract: The extensive use of Internet of Things (IoT) devices in healthcare, industrial, and smart city systems has greatly expanded the area of attack to cybercriminals. Of these threats, zero-day attacks are the most harmful as they use unidentified weaknesses and avoid use of traditional signature-based methods of detection. To overcome this dilemma, there is a need to have adaptive and smart solutions that can detect new trends of malicious activities in real time. This study introduces a software-based system of zero-day attack detection in the IoT networks through the combination of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) and online learning schemes. The IoT environment is defined in the form of a dynamic graph, with devices being the nodes, and communication links being the edges that allow the system to reflect structural dependencies and contextual information. The GNNs are used to learn high-level embeddings on the network activity, whereas the online learning part constantly updates the detection model with new traffic patterns revealed. This dynamic mechanism increases resistance to the changing threats without the need to have to manually update the signature. Simulated traffic assessments on an IoT-based traffic simulation show that the proposed framework exhibits excellent detection accuracy and less false-positive than the conventional evaluation techniques on anomaly detection. Its software-based design guarantees the scalability of the software and its compatibility with various IoT platforms, which makes it a suitable solution to a real-life implementation. The proposed research integrates the concepts of representation learning on graphs with continuous model adaptation, thus offering a practical approach to reducing the threats of the occurrence of zero-day attacks in an IoT ecosystem.

title: Smart door lock design and development using the pahl and beitz approach

abstract: Security vulnerabilities in conventional locks and existing smart locks necessitate innovative solutions that integrate robust authentication mechanisms. This study addresses the research gap by developing a smart door lock system that uniquely combines Indonesia's government-issued e-KTP (embedded with an RFID chip) and a capacitive touch sensor for multi-factor authentication, enhancing security while ensuring universal accessibility. The design process employs the Pahl and Beitz systematic engineering methodology, emphasizing iterative optimization through planning, conceptual design, embodiment design, and detail design phases. Key specifications, including e-KTP compatibility, cost-effectiveness <IDR 1 million, and energy efficiency, were prioritized. Prototype evaluations revealed that the final design achieved superior functionality, scoring 87/100 in a multi-criteria assessment. The assessment considered components, space, aesthetics, cost, and manufacturability. The system integrates an Arduino Nano Microcontroller, a 9V battery with a 17-day lifespan, and IoT connectivity for real-time feedback. Comparative analysis demonstrates a 40–60% cost reduction compared to commercial alternatives, alongside tamper-resistant advantages from e-KTP integration system, modularity potential, and rechargeable battery. This study underscores the viability of leveraging national ID systems in IoT security frameworks, offering policymakers and manufacturers actionable insights for scalable, standardized smart home solutions.

title: A NbOI2-based flexible piezoelectric sensor for acoustic signal acquisition and gesture-controlled human-machine interaction systems.

abstract: Driven by the demand for low-power sensing in wearable electronics and intelligent human-machine interaction, two-dimensional piezoelectric materials, which combine self-powered capability, mechanical flexibility, and integration compatibility, provide a promising material platform for high-performance flexible sensors. In this work, a flexible piezoelectric sensor based on two-dimensional NbOI2 was constructed on a polyimide substrate. The device exhibits stable and repeatable piezoelectric responses over bending angles from 30° to 75° and operating frequencies from 0.47 to 2.10 Hz. At a bending angle of 75°, the peak output current reaches 167.01 pA. Under the conditions of a bending angle of 45° and a bending frequency of 1.31 Hz, after more than 1000 bending cycles, the device retains approximately 95.0% of its initial output performance, demonstrating excellent electromechanical conversion capability and mechanical durability. Furthermore, the device enables acoustic signal acquisition, mechanical motion recognition, and gesture-triggered control and was successfully integrated into a human-machine interaction system for smart-home control and robotic-hand manipulation. This work highlights the potential of NbOI2-based flexible piezoelectric sensors in self-powered sensing, acoustic acquisition, and intelligent interaction, providing a practical reference for the integration of two-dimensional piezoelectric materials into flexible electronic systems.

title: Research on Multimodal Interaction of Embodied Perception Agent for Industrial Design Based on LoRA Lightweight Training
venue: 2026 International Conference on Blockchain Technology and Foundation Models (BTFM)

abstract: To address key challenges in industrial design—high large-model deployment costs, inadequate multimodal perception/emotional adaptation in human-computer interaction, and poor design-manufacturing collaboration —this study proposes an LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation)-based lightweight embodied perception agent architecture integrated with a multimodal perception-fusion interaction mechanism, aligning with the Greater Bay Area’s trend of embodied intelligence technology implementation and industrial integration. Targeting Guangdong’s county-level manufacturing and Lingnan characteristic industries (e.g., smart home appliances, pan-home furnishings), the architecture adopts a three-layer design (multimodal perception, LoRA training, and interaction decision layers): the multimodal perception layer incorporates visual, auditory, emotional perception, and drawing understanding modules for comprehensive collection and parsing of diverse design data; the LoRA training layer optimizes low-rank matrix dimensions and fine-tuning strategies for industrial design datasets, enabling high-precision training with 1% labeled data and compatibility with county-level enterprises’ lightweight computing resources (supported by Guangdong’s “computing power vouchers”), thereby realizing lightweight deployment; the interaction decision layer integrates county-level manufacturing constraints (e.g., mold processing capabilities) and leverages LoRA’s domain adaptation capability to convert multimodal perception data into manufacturable schemes, achieving designmanufacturing collaboration. A 100,000-sample industrial design dataset was constructed, with training parameters optimized on the Stable Diffusion (SD) 1.5 base model and an attention mechanism adopted for multimodal feature fusion.Experimental results demonstrate this approach cuts large-model computing power costs by 70%, boosts industrial design task efficiency by 45%, achieves 89.2% design accuracy, and shortens the traditional 3–6-month design cycle to within 2 weeks. Pilot tests in Shunde, Zhongshan, and other Guangdong enterprises confirm significant improvements in product manufacturability and customer satisfaction. Aligning with Guangdong’s Action Plan for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Empowering High-Quality Manufacturing Development and the “Hundred-Thousand-Ten Thousand Project”, this study fills the gap in LoRA technology adaptation for industrial design, providing a lightweight, scenario-specific solution for the intelligent transformation of county-level manufacturing and fostering in-depth synergy between embodied intelligence theory and the industrial design industry.

title: Design and Implementation of an IoT-Based Smart Home System Using the Matter Protocol
venue: 2026 11th International Conference on Applying New Technology in Green Buildings (ATiGB)

abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has significantly accelerated the development of smart home systems, enabling automation, energy efficiency, and enhanced user experience. However, the lack of interoperability among heterogeneous devices and platforms remains a major challenge, resulting in fragmented ecosystems and limited scalability. To address these issues, the Matter protocol has emerged as a unified, IP-based connectivity standard for smart home environments. This paper presents a comprehensive study of the Matter protocol, including its architecture, communication mechanisms, and security model. A practical IoT-based smart home system is designed and implemented using ESP32 platforms and the Matter SDK. The system integrates multiple devices such as smart lighting, switches, smart plugs, and environmental sensors, supporting crossplatform interaction across different ecosystems. Experimental evaluation is conducted under real-world conditions, focusing on interoperability, latency, system stability, and security. The results show that the proposed system achieves reliable crossplatform compatibility, stable network performance, low communication latency, and secure device authentication. Additionally, the system maintains core functionality even under limited network conditions, demonstrating strong robustness. These findings confirm that the Matter protocol is a promising solution for building scalable, secure, and interoperable next-generation smart home systems.

title: Ultrahigh-sensitivity bias-free Sb2S3/Si van der Waals heterojunction photodetector enabling indoor illuminance monitoring
reason: title: not about third-party code on a smart-home hub or gateway
abstract: The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled smart home systems necessitates next-generation indoor optical sensors with ultralow power consumption, ambient-light adaptability, and system-level integrability. Addressing this technological imperative, this study proposed a self-powered broadband photodetector (PD) through vertical integration of a hydrothermally synthesized Sb 2 S 3 single crystal with a commercial Si substrate. The Sb 2 S 3 /Si heterojunction PD showcases a maximum responsivity of 172 mA/W, a detectivity of 10 10 Jones, and sub-millisecond response dynamics (172/160 μ s rising/ falling) upon 720 nm illumination at 0 V bias, outperforming other Sb 2 S 3 competitors. Such exceptional zero-bias operation enables direct compatibility with energy-autonomous IoT nodes. Particularly, the device ’ s spectral alignment with indoor lighting harmonics and long-term drift-free operation establishes its viability for intelligent lighting control, occupancy detection, and low power consumption in residential IoT ecosystems. The synthesis innovation of Sb 2 S 3 monocrystalline structures provides a scalable pathway toward batteryless smart sensors for sustainable home automation.

title: Real-Time Edge Computing for Object Classification: Deploying Lightweight CNNs on Raspberry Pi with Firebase Analytics

abstract: IoT-based Smart home environments are becoming more and more dependent on intelligent perception systems to provide context-sensitive and adaptive behavior. Classification of objects is important in enabling such systems to respond and comprehend daily interactions. A real-time object classification system using a pre-trained MobileNetV2 CNN, which will be deployed on an edge device, a resource-constrained machine, the Raspberry Pi. The system proposed categorizes everyday household items, such as water bottles, mobile phones, mugs, pens, and computer mice, based on the images of a USB camera. Transfer learning is utilized to optimize the MobileNetV2 model on a dataset created based on Open images database, which contains 1,188 images with 5 object classes. The trained model is invoked on the Raspberry Pi to carry out real-time inference and results of classification along with confidence scores, FPS, inference time, and timestamps are sent to a Firebase Realtime Database to be logged and analyzed. Experimental findings on the classification accuracy show a strong classification accuracy of 99% with little misclassification indicating the efficiency of the proposed approach. Optimized real-time performance and compatibility with reliable cloud integration are attained by the system, thus it is applicable in smart home and internet-of-things applications requiring reliable and low-latency object recognition on edge devices.

title: An MQTT-enabled IoT architecture for smart curtain systems with embedded edge-cloud integration
venue: International Conference on Optics, Electronics, and Communication Engineering

abstract: To address the issues of delayed response, fragmented functionality, and poor compatibility in conventional curtain and window control systems, this paper proposes and implements an intelligent curtain-window coordination system based on multi-sensor integration. The system utilizes an STM32 microcontroller as the central processor, integrating temperature, humidity, light, and rain sensors, and employs an ESP8266 Wi-Fi module to establish communication with a cloud-based IoT platform. Leveraging the lightweight MQTT protocol, the system supports real-time environmental data upload and command downlink. A WeChat Mini Program is developed as the client interface, allowing users to remotely monitor environmental conditions and control curtains and windows in real time. Compared with traditional single-function control devices, the proposed system achieves seamless integration of curtain movement, window actuation, and environmental sensing, while enabling closed-loop management across cloud and mobile terminals through a low-cost architecture. With its modular design, stable communication, and responsive performance, the system is well-suited for smart control scenarios in residential, office, and greenhouse environments, offering a scalable and cost-effective pathway for smart home system development.

title: Investigating the Adoption of Smart Home Solutions in Oman
venue: 2026 International Conference on Sustainable Engineering and Digital Innovation (ICSEDI)

abstract: The adoption of smart home technologies has gained momentum globally due to their potential to enhance comfort, improve safety, and increase energy efficiency within residential environments. This study investigates the uptake of smart home technologies in Oman, focusing on their impact on users’ quality of life and identifying the key barriers hindering widespread implementation. The research reviews the current state of smart home systems and evaluates their contribution to sustainability and energy conservation. Key concerns such as privacy risks, cyber threats, high installation costs, and device compatibility are also addressed. Additionally, the study explores user-related factors like ease of use, accessibility, and system interoperability, which significantly influence adoption behavior. A mixed-method approach combining surveys and interviews was used to collect qualitative and quantitative data on user experiences and perceptions. The final phase of the study presents recommendations for improving technology adoption by enhancing security measures, reducing financial burdens, and promoting device standardization. This research provides valuable insights for stakeholders aiming to integrate smart home technologies into Oman's digital transformation initiatives and highlights their role in creating secure, efficient, and intelligent living environments.

title: SMART CITIES IN PRACTICE: IOT-ENABLED CITIZEN ENGAGEMENT AND LOCAL SERVICE DELIVERY

abstract: The development of smart cities also marks a paradigm change in the governance of cities with the Internet of Things (IoT) was acting as a booster to the participation of citizens and better services delivery. This paper seeks to interrogate how IoT-based infrastructures change the way local governments operate by making decision-making participatory, city operations efficient and bolster citizen trust. The study is based on the multi-case comparative design that takes its qualitative data at the city level in various geographical regions. The evidence base consists of interviews with local stakeholders on municipal level, interpretation of IoT platforms, and policy and technical documentation. The results show that platforms enabled by IoT enable real-time communication between rulers and the ruled, decreased response-time in service-delivery, and promoted transparency by means of data-driven governance. In addition, the uses of IoT enable citizens to co-design solutions in the fields of waste and transportation, mobility and energy efficiency, in tandem with the general principles of sustainable smart governance. Technical issues like the protection of privacy, compatibility of IoT standards, and scalability of solutions have been detected, and the federated data frameworks and lightweight protocols should be considered as an integration. It is concluded that the idea of citizen participation through IoT contributes to a better-performing city not only in terms of city responsiveness but also supports the concepts of Industry 5.0, such as the illusion of an urban ecosystem that is human-centric, collaborative, resilient in nature. In four cities, citizen reports rose 106143% waste collectors costs declined 25%, and citizen trust levels rose 32 percentage points (4678%), showing measurable improvement in governance through IoT enabled citizen participation.
